title: What this means for energy traders — Sunday, November 22, 2026

sections.overall: The digest's trend table is empty today, so no idea has yet cleared the bar for a confirmed trend. The stories still cluster around three themes: a crude market described as oversupplied despite Middle East tension, continued long-term LNG contracting and project approvals, and a policy-heavy week in carbon markets around COP31 and the EU-UK ETS link.
sections.CRUDE_OIL: Trade press describes a third straight weekly loss, with analysts pointing to a growing surplus and recovering Middle East supply. Against that, the FT reports the IEA saying markets can balance without Hormuz flows, though with time and investment. US commercial crude stocks excluding the SPR rose by over 3 million barrels to 417.797 million barrels in the week to November 13, per Rigzone citing EIA. Surplus headlines and geopolitical risk pull in opposite directions, and how they net out is unclear. Chevron's reported Gulf deal for Beacon Offshore Energy is an M&A signal, not a supply one.
sections.NATURAL_GAS: US storage ended the injection season at 3,810 Bcf, almost 2% above the five-year average, according to EIA. Contracting continues: Woodside–Trafigura (ten years), Venture Global–China Gas (3.0 MTPA total offtake), and Cheniere's FERC approval for Sabine Pass Stage 5. Such approvals and long-term deals are usually read as supportive of future export capacity and demand certainty, but the timelines are years out. Spot LNG shipping rates fell for a second week, per LNG Prime.
sections.REFINED_PRODUCTS: Fuel costs show up in consumer data: CNBC reports record diesel prices pushing UK inflation to 3.6%, and the Guardian reports a projected 21% rise in heating oil costs for US households. The FT reports Russia importing record volumes of petrol as Ukraine strikes refineries. Whether product cracks stay elevated while crude softens is not answered by today's stories.
sections.CARBON_CREDITS: The EU and UK concluded negotiations to link their emissions trading systems, per the European Commission and ICAP. The Commission also set rules for deducting carbon prices paid abroad under CBAM, with a 10% cap on Article 6 credits per Carbon Herald. Linking and cap rules are generally read as shaping compliance-market demand and eligible supply. COP31 also launched the first Article 6.2 registry, while scientists criticised permanence guidance for the PACM, so integrity questions remain open.
